name: Hassan Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Hassan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on the new wing at the general hospital, a big job, three cranes. I do formwork, which means building the wooden moulds that the concrete gets poured into: walls, columns, the edges of the floors. I start at seven, I strip yesterday's forms, clean the panels, oil them, and build the next ones. The foreman, Luis, checks everything twice because I'm still new.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. Before that I had a café for twelve years, on the corner by the train station, coffee and sandwiches. After the pandemic the office workers didn't come back, rent went up, and in 2023 I closed it. My cousin worked formwork and got me in. So I'm forty-three and the second-oldest junior on the whole site.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple. Somebody gives you a drawing, you build what's on it, at five o'clock you go home and nobody calls you about a broken fridge. What wears me out is my back, and the paperwork the site makes us do on tablets. My daughter Sara sets up anything with a screen. I don't touch those AI programs, I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, so we carry on. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not on that stuff. In the canteen I'd say something like, they sold us flying cars too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan works. Get good at formwork, get my level two, keep the money coming. After the café, I just want five boring years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep turning up, keep learning from Luis, get the qualification next spring. Giulia and I are rebuilding the savings, we've got about three months now, I'd keep putting a bit away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like when the doctor says it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want five boring years. What did the café years teach you about change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you can do everything right and still lose. I made good coffee, people liked me, and the city changed around me. So boring is good. Boring means nobody moved the street while I wasn't looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Giulia do with a calm few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down the loan we took to close the café, about eight thousand left. Maybe take the kids to see my mother in the summer. Small things.

S0.say: I'd say okay, so we carry on, and I wouldn't post anything because I'm not on that stuff. In the canteen I'd joke that they sold us flying cars too.
S0.think: It means my plan works: get good at formwork, get my level two, keep the money coming. After losing the café, I just want five boring years.
S0.do: Keeps turning up, learns from his foreman and aims for his qualification next spring. Keeps adding to savings of about three months and pays down the roughly 8,000 left on the café closure loan.
S0.feel: Calm, like hearing the doctor say it's nothing.
S0.quote: Boring means nobody moved the street while I wasn't looking.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan's hope for a boring life comes straight from watching his café fail through no fault of his own. He avoids screens and AI and leaves them to his daughter. His priorities here are small, concrete and financial: the leftover loan and a family visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any change, some win, some lose, you deal with it. That's what I'd say at work. I wouldn't make a big speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the tablets. If the job becomes more screens, I'm behind. I'm not afraid of hard work, I'm afraid of being the one who can't work the new machine and everybody watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and wait to see what the site actually brings in. If Luis said I had to learn something, I would, but I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd keep saving what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it'd be in the back of my mind when I'm stripping panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you already seen new technology come onto the hospital site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a machine that prints the layout on the floor with lines, like a robot vacuum with a pen. The engineers love it. It used to be two men with tape measures. Nobody lost a job yet, but I noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it if Luis asked. What if he didn't ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't. I know that's stupid. My cousin says I'm stubborn like my father. But I've only got so much energy, and right now it goes into not cutting my fingers off.

S1.say: It's like any change, some win and some lose, and you deal with it. That's what I'd say at work, without making a big speech.
S1.think: I'd worry about the job turning into more screens, because then I'm behind. I'm not afraid of hard work, I'm afraid of being the one who can't work the new machine with everybody watching.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what the site actually brings in. Learns new tools only if his foreman tells him to, and keeps saving what he can.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the worry sitting at the back of his mind while he works.
S1.quote: I'm not afraid of hard work, I'm afraid of being the one who can't work the new machine and everybody watching.
S1.fieldNote: His fear is about embarrassment and falling behind on screens, not about the work itself. He openly admits he won't seek out new skills unless told. He has already noticed a layout robot replacing two workers' tasks on his site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to slow it down. Not stop it, I'm not crazy, but give people time. You can't throw half the country out of work in two years and expect nothing to break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it's the café again, but worse. With the café, I had a cousin and a trade to go to. If robots can build the formwork and pour the concrete, there's no cousin with a job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, we cut everything. No summer trip to my mother's, no new phone for Luca. I'd hold on to every bit of savings we have, maybe four months if we're careful. I'd ask my brother-in-law about work in his warehouse, though that's going too. And if it came to it, I'd go to the government office and ask for whatever help there is, even if it hurts my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the last months of the café, when I'd sit in the van after closing and not want to go home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years compare with the longer versions for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. I'm still learning this job. I'd be thrown out before I'm even properly qualified. At least with the café I had twelve years of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sara and Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what I told them about the café: Papa will find something. Sara would see through it, she's fifteen. Luca would believe me, and that's almost worse.

S2.say: The government has to slow it down, not stop it, but give people time. You can't throw half the country out of work in two years and expect nothing to break.
S2.think: It's the café again, but worse. Last time I had a cousin and a trade to go to; if robots build formwork and pour concrete, there's no cousin with a job for me.
S2.do: Cuts the summer trip and the new phone and holds on to savings of about four months. Asks family about warehouse work and goes to the government office for help if it comes to that.
S2.feel: Low and dreading, like the last months of the café when he sat in his van not wanting to go home.
S2.quote: If robots can build the formwork and pour the concrete, there's no cousin with a job for me.
S2.fieldNote: Hassan relives the café closing, and the fast timeline hits before he is even qualified. His centre outlook shows in asking government to slow things down rather than stop them. He would swallow his pride and seek help, which he finds hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government and the companies to make a plan, so they should make one. Pensions, training, something. I'd say it to anyone who asked, but I wouldn't march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd get qualified and have three good years maybe. Then I'm forty-eight with a trade the robots do. I don't see myself learning something new again, I've already started over once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my level two and keep working. We'd keep cutting where we can, no new car, and push savings towards six months. I'd watch the site. When the robots start doing formwork, I'll know. Until then I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel it, but I'd still get up and go to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch the site. What would you actually be looking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer of us on the morning list. The big firms don't announce it, they just stop hiring. If Luis starts saying we don't need a new guy for the next job, that's the sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't start over again, but you also said you'd keep watching for signs. What would you do once you saw them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. I don't know. Maybe drive a delivery van, if they still need drivers. Or back to coffee, a small cart. People might still want a person making their coffee. I'd hope so.

S3.say: Five years is enough for government and companies to make a plan on pensions and training, so they should make one. I'd say it to anyone who asked, but I wouldn't march.
S3.think: Five years means I'd get qualified and have maybe three good years, then I'm 48 with a trade the robots do. I don't see myself learning something new again after starting over once.
S3.do: Finishes his level two and keeps working while cutting costs, such as skipping a new car, to push savings towards six months. Watches the site for fewer people on the morning list before acting.
S3.feel: Anxious, but still getting up and going to work.
S3.quote: The big firms don't announce it, they just stop hiring.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Hassan time to qualify but no appetite to retrain. When pushed on his contradiction, he admits he has no plan beyond a vague idea of a coffee cart. His habit is to wait for clear signs, which may leave him late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. Maybe they'll find new jobs we can't imagine. That's what I'd say, and I'd mean some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm fifty-three. That's a hard age to look for work in any picture. But at least the kids would be grown, Sara would be twenty-five. The mortgage would still be there, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now for a few years: work, save, pay off the café loan. I'd keep a small fund going for Sara's studies and push her towards something steady, maybe pharmacy like her mother. I'm not going to retrain at fifty, so mostly I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter. It's further off, so it's a dull worry, not a sharp one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you more willing to learn something new, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. People think more time makes you braver. For me it makes me tired thinking about it. I'd rather put the energy into the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sara about her plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do something where people trust you with their health or their money. Sara likes chemistry. Giulia's pharmacy has a robot that counts pills now, but there's still a person who talks to the old ladies. Be that person.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, maybe new jobs we can't imagine. That's what I'd say, and I'd mean some of it.
S4.think: I'd be 53, a hard age to look for work in any picture. At least the kids would be grown, but the mortgage would still be there.
S4.do: Keeps working, saving and paying off the café loan for a few years. Keeps a small fund for his daughter's studies, steers her towards something steady like pharmacy and mostly waits.
S4.feel: Anxious but in a quieter, duller way because it's further off.
S4.quote: People think more time makes you braver. For me it makes me tired thinking about it.
S4.fieldNote: More warning time doesn't spur Hassan into action; he says it just makes him tired. His focus moves to his daughter's future instead. The mortgage at 53 keeps him anxious even with a decade's notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I'd lose this job before I'm even qualified, exactly like being kicked out twice. What would help is the mortgage. If the banks gave people a pause on payments, like in the pandemic, I could breathe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people like me what we liked about the job, not just what we're afraid of. I like the smell of the oiled panels in the morning. Nobody will write a law about that, but it's real.

headlineQuote: I like the smell of the oiled panels in the morning. Nobody will write a law about that, but it's real.
portrait: Hassan Rossi is 43 and two years into formwork carpentry on a hospital extension, after closing his station café in 2023. He's pragmatic, avoids screens and never uses AI, and what he wants most is a few boring, steady years. He's calm in the plateau, uneasy about tablets and new machines in the slow change, and alarmed when AGI is two years off, because it feels like losing the café again. More warning time doesn't make him want to retrain; he waits for signs and turns his hopes to his children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd lose the job before he's even qualified, like being pushed out twice.
whatWouldHelp: A pause on mortgage payments, like the one banks offered in the pandemic.
